lessons.title: Fiber vs Microwave vs Laser — The Physics of Speed

children.text: Fiber optic cable looks like the obvious choice for anything data related. It is not the fastest way to move a signal between two points, and in a business built on microseconds, that gap matters enough to justify building microwave towers on rooftops across Mumbai.
Light Is Slower in Glass Than You Think

markDefs.definition: A number describing how much slower light travels through a given medium compared to a vacuum. Speed through the medium equals c, the speed of light in vacuum, divided by the refractive index.

children.text: Light in a vacuum travels at about 3.0 x 10^8 metres per second, the constant everyone learned in school as c. Light travelling through the glass core of a fiber optic cable does not move that fast. Glass has a

of roughly 1.5, and a signal's speed through any medium equals c divided by that medium's refractive index. The result: light inside a fiber optic cable moves at only about two thirds of its vacuum speed, closer to 2.0 x 10^8 metres per second.

children.text: Why HFT Firms Still Use Microwave and Laser

Speed through the medium is only half the story. A fiber route between two data centres has to follow roads, ducts, and existing cable paths, which is almost always longer than the straight-line distance between them. A microwave or laser link, by contrast, can run in a straight line from rooftop to rooftop. Some infrastructure vendors offer exactly this kind of direct microwave or laser hop between NSE's and BSE's data centres in Mumbai, since the straight-line distance between the two facilities is short enough that a direct line-of-sight link offers a real, measurable edge over any fiber route forced to wind through the city.

body.text: Microwave and laser links trade reliability for speed. Rain fade can degrade a microwave signal during heavy rain, and fog or haze can block a laser link entirely. This is exactly why the redundancy principle from the previous chapter shows up again here: firms running latency-critical microwave or laser links almost always keep a fiber path as backup, accepting the fiber's slower speed in exchange for a connection that keeps working through a Mumbai monsoon.

body.title: Work the route
body.prompt: A fiber route between two data centres is 10 km long, since fiber must follow roads and ducts, and light travels through it at about 2.0 x 10^8 m/s. A microwave link between the same two data centres is a direct 6 km line of sight, with the signal travelling at close to the speed of light in air, about 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. Roughly how many microseconds does the microwave link save compared to the fiber route?
body.explanation: Fiber time equals 10,000 metres divided by 2.0 x 10^8 m/s, which is 50 microseconds. Microwave time equals 6,000 metres divided by 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, which is 20 microseconds. The microwave link saves about 30 microseconds, purely from taking a shorter, more direct path through a faster medium.

body.text: In this business, the shortest path and the fastest medium are two different problems, and a firm that only solves one of them is leaving speed on the table.

points: Light travels slower through fiber optic glass, about 0.67c, than through air, close to 1c, because of the medium's refractive index.
A fiber route's real disadvantage often has two parts: the slower medium, and a longer physical path forced by roads and ducts, compared to a microwave or laser link's straight line.
Microwave links need relay towers roughly every 50 km and are vulnerable to rain fade. Laser links are even more vulnerable to fog and haze.
Because of that vulnerability, firms typically run microwave or laser as the fast primary path and keep fiber as a slower, but far more reliable, backup.
